title: The shortest psalm (Psalm 116 [117])
hookLine: two verses: praise the Lord, all nations

cards: Some psalms go on for pages. And then there's this one. You could say it while the kettle boils, or while a traffic light changes.
Two verses, under thirty words in the Douay: the shortest psalm in the Psalter. And in those few words it invites the whole planet. Not one people, not one city, not one church.

teach.h: TWO VERSES: THE INVITE AND THE REASON.
teach.b: Here is the whole thing, in the Douay-Rheims: "O praise the Lord, all ye nations: praise him, all ye people. For his mercy is confirmed upon us: and the truth of the Lord remaineth for ever." That's the psalm.
First, the shape. Verse one is the invitation, as wide as it can be: all nations, all peoples. Verse two gives the reason, in two old Hebrew words that run all through the Psalms.

teach.h: MERCY AND TRUTH: LOVE THAT HOLDS.
teach.b: Mercy is chesed, the steady, loyal love that keeps a promise. Truth is emet, faithfulness, the thing you can lean your weight on.
So the whole world is invited to praise because God's love holds, and God's faithfulness lasts. Second, where it sits.

teach.h: SUNG AT PASSOVER, THEN AND NOW.
teach.b: Like yesterday's psalm, it belongs to the Hallel, the psalms of praise sung at Passover and the great feasts, and it's still sung in Jewish worship today. Third, who picked it up.
Saint Paul quotes it in his letter to the Romans, to say the good news was meant for the nations, not one people alone.

teach.h: O PRAISE THE LORD, ALL YE NATIONS.
teach.b: The Church kept singing it in Latin, Laudate Dominum, omnes gentes. Mozart set it to music, and pilgrims at Taizé sing it over and over.
A Catholic can pray it at Vespers, a Jewish family sings it at Passover, and both are singing the same two verses about everyone.

how: Catholics pray Psalm 116 [117] in the Liturgy of the Hours, and it is often sung in Latin as Laudate Dominum; some pray it through the day as a short prayer of praise.

games.q: you're writing a psalm with room for only two verses. the first invites all nations to praise. what goes in the second?
o: a list of what the nations must do first.
the reason: God's mercy holds and his truth lasts.
a warning for anyone who won't join in.
games.why: the second verse is just the reason: "his mercy is confirmed upon us: and the truth of the Lord remaineth for ever."

practice: If you pray, say the two verses slowly three times: once as they are, once picturing a country you've never visited, with people waking up there right now, and once picturing someone near you who is nothing like you.
If you don't pray, just hold those three pictures in the quiet: here, far away, and next door.

wordCard.voice: Laudate Dominum. Latin for praise the Lord, the shortest psalm in the whole Psalter: two verses that invite all nations. Today's word.

orig.note: Latin: praise the Lord, the psalm's first words in the Vulgate, set to music by Mozart.
